title: The Art of Changing Your Mind
author: Ian Hallett
summary: Ian Hallett argues that the real leadership question is not whether to change your mind but whether the people watching can tell if you are learning or flinching. He contrasts Duolingo's CEO rescinding an AI-first rule after staff feedback with the AI company chiefs who walked back jobs predictions while heading toward public listings. Both reversals were defensible, yet one read as responding to evidence and the other as responding to bankers. He offers a four-part test: what specifically changed, whether the new position costs you something, whether you own the old position, and whether the direction is still the same. He also warns that constant reversals are just a failure to decide, and closes with an exercise of running the test on one still-active decision you suspect was wrong.
points: Your organisation judges what a reversal says about how decisions get made, not whether you were right the first time.
Learning names the new evidence, costs the leader something, owns the old call, and keeps the strategic direction intact.
Flinching blames misinterpretation or conditions and reaches for vague language because pressure, not evidence, changed.
Reversals must stay rare and evidenced or they signal a leader who has stopped deciding.
Quietly letting a wrong decision fade teaches everyone that decisions here simply evaporate.
quotes: Von Ahn did not change his mind about AI. He still believes in it, still wants to hire people who use it well.
Two changes of mind, weeks apart, both defensible. One read as a leader responding to evidence. The other read as a leader responding to bankers.
Remember: your organisation is not judging whether you were right the first time. It is judging what your reversal tells them about how decisions get made here.
Learning names the new information. Von Ahn could point to what his staff were telling him and to code he could not reliably debug.
Nobody believes a reversal that happens to make life easier. Von Ahn abandoned a policy he had announced publicly, which cost him.
A leader who changes position every time the evidence wobbles has not learned anything; they have just stopped deciding.
So make reversals rare, so that they mean something when they come. Evidence them, so that somebody can check your reasoning. And own them, because otherwise everyone will guess whether you noticed.
